LESTER VS. BUTLER.

Motion by the United States Attorney to Dismiss the Actions.

NEW YORK, August 31.—The United States District Attorney this afternoon began the preparation of argument on the motion to dismiss certain actions now pending in the United States Circuit Court against General Benjamin F. Butler, to recover in all $475,000 damages. John H. Lester, now of New York, but formerly of Virginia, has two actions, one for $75,000 and the other for $100,000 damages. During the war it was discovered that Lester assisted in the manufacture of arms for the Confederate Government. He was tried by court martial and sentenced to ten years imprisonment with ball and chain, and his property was confiscated. Francis M. Fisk has an action for $300,000 damages for property, including machinery, molasses, household utensils, etc., confiscated by order of the President. A motion to dismiss will be made, on the ground that the defendant acted in accordance with a proclamation of the President in confiscating the property of plaintiff, and was therefore not liable to prosecution for damages.

Interesting Discovery.

The St. Petersburg correspondent of the London Standard reports that some interesting discoveries have been made at Kelver, where, in excavating ground for the new harbor, the hulls of several ships long buried in the earth, have been laid bare. Four Russian men of war, of considerable dimensions—120 to 180 feet long—have it, is said, been identified. From the inscription, "Olonets, 1711," on one of the cannons found, it seems that the ships were wrecked after that date, and the fact is curious, as showing how rapidly the water has receded. In old times the sea evidently came up to the walls of the town, which then must have presented a singularly picturesque appearance, with its quaint red-tiled houses, perched high on the rock above. At present there is half a mile of dry land between the walls and the harbor, and where great ships rode not very long ago the locomotive now runs between rows of wharves and merchants' offices.

The Situation at the National Capital.

WASHINGTON, October 7th.—The Senators of both parties to-night are averse to being interviewed as to what they will or may do in the organization of the Senate. There is a sentiment of concession on both sides, but no Senator knows just how far it will go, and he does not like to express an opinion which may embarrass him when he come to vote. It is freely admitted that there must be some concession and compromise, but what shape it will take cannot be foretold. Some suggest that a President pro tem, be elected for the express purpose of swearing in the new Senators, his term of office to be until next year, and after that an organization can be effected. There are precedents for this. The Senate has in the past elected a President for a specific duty or for a designated period of time. On one occasion a President was elected for one day. There are at least three Democratic Senators who are in favor of conceding the President to the Republicans if they will accord to the Democrats the Secretaryship and half of the committees, and let the remainder of the organization stand as now. One of the most influential Democrats in the Senate to-night expressed himself in favor of this plan. He said he was satisfied that if the Democrats would accord the President to the Republicans, an amicable agreement can be reached in a short time, and the Senate organized by a unanimous vote; but if, on the other hand, the Democrats take advantage of their temporary majority to elect a President he believed the Republicans would fight on the question of Secretary, and the remainder of the organization to the last day of the Forty-seventh Congress. This Senator said that if another deadlock arises it will run, there is no telling how long, and will block legislation at the regular session of Congress. This would be ill-timed and disgraceful, said this Senator; therefore he considered that the easiest and best plan is to give the Republicans the office they most desire, which is President of the Senate. The President and the Pastors.

WASHINGTON, October 7th.—The pastors of this city, accompanied by the Maryland Lutheran Synod, in session here, called on President Arthur this afternoon at his residence. Dr. Chester, pastor of the Metropolitan Presbyterian Church, was spokesman for the visitors, and read the address. The President responded substantially as follows: "I am glad to meet you, gentlemen, yet it is with deep sorrow, under circumstances which have sadly devolved such momentous duties upon me. In the performance of these duties, as chief of a God-fearing and religious people, I appreciate my dependence upon their moral support and approval and upon the Divine blessing and guidance. I thank you cordially for the assurances of your support, for your kind expressions of sympathy and confidence." At the conclusion of President Arthur's response the visitors were individually introduced and shook hands with the President. The party then retired, evidently much pleased with the interview.

War Among the Authors.

NEW YORK, October 7th. — Joaquin Miller writes in reply to McKee Rankin's claim to having written "The Danites," and paid the poet merely for the use of his name: "The books which have borne my name were executed by patient toil. They have elicited from reviewers many severe criticisms. I have been charged, and perhaps justly, with many faults and follies; but the charge of want of originality is not one of them. In the 10,000 pages of comment upon me and my works, I have yet to find the accusation that I received the honor and the pay for the task performed by another. When, therefore, a man like McKee Rankin makes a charge of this kind, I find myself in the position of one who, when about to sit down to his boiled joint, finds that a dog has stolen it, has munched it out of palatable shape, rolled it in the mire, and claiming proprietorship. The exact result of such an incident is that morally the joint is the man's, but actually when he comes to look at it he doesn't care to own it, or to engage in a canine fight to prove that he ever did."

The circumstances leading up to this point are as follows. Between nine and ten o'clock last night the Chief was informed that Nelms was in the city, and had made arrangements to be taken across the river in a skiff at midnight.
Without loss of time a party was made up, and headed by the Chief, went across the river in a skiff, landing at the Teenie Vance place, just above the old government light. They waited in a laborer's cabin near the bank for some time, watching for the skiff, but it failed to arrive when expected, and the entire party, with the exception of the Chief and Captain Hackett, returned to the city, believing they were on the wrong scent. The Chief declared his intention of remaining all night, and arranged with the balance of the party to fire his gun at daylight as a signal for them to come for him. The Chief and Captain Hackett took turns at watching. At half past one o'clock, while the Chief was on the look out he
HEARD THE SOUND OF OARS and discerned the dim outlines of a skiff rapidly approaching the bank. Dashing back to the cabin Captain Hackett was warned, and a laborer named A. Bodkins, who was present, was requested to go along and be ready to disarm the criminal in case he should surrender without resistance. The trio stole softly down toward the bank, which was sloping at this point, and stopped behind a log, about forty yards from the water's edge. Captain Hackett and Bodkins stooped behind the log, but the Chief, who discovered they had been seen, threw aside all reserve, and called out:
“Halloo, boys! Got any whisky aboard?”
“Who are you?” demanded one of the party.
“Oh, we're working for the railroad!” the Chief answered; and then asked:
“Where are you from?”
“Across the river,” was the answer.
“And where are you going to?” was again asked.
“We want to make out toward the railroad,” was the reply.
The Chief fearing the skiff party would recognize his voice, requested Bodkins to do the talking. That gentleman told the party they could not get out through the course they were pointing, but had better come near to where they were, as that was the best way to the high road. The party, four in number, walked up the bank, making directly for the spot where the officers stood. When they had approached within ten feet of him, Chief Davis presented his gun at the head of Riley, the uncle of Nelms, who was carrying a shotgun, and apparently was the only one of them armed.
“Surrender,” he cried, “or you are a dead man; I am an officer of the law.”
“I surrender,” said Riley, dropping the breech of the gun to the ground.
At this instant the Chief's eye detected one of the party who he at once thought to be Nelms, slipping his right hand around to his hip and at the same moment was startled to learn that Captain Hackett's gun covered the same man his did, and that Nelms was left uncovered. Swinging his gun around so as to bear on the murderer, he commanded him to surrender. Nelms never uttered a word, but crouching himself close to the ground, began slowly walking backward, with his hand still creeping toward his pistol, and his eyes staring fixedly into those of Chief Davis. The latter reiterated his demand, when Nelms suddenly stepped forward. Mr. Davis had advanced upon Nelms as the latter had retreated, and was within a few yards of him at the moment. He was not quite certain that it was the man he wanted, the shadows of the night.

but he felt sure enough of it to be satisfied that there was no time to lose. He pulled trigger, thinking to cripple his man, but the load of shot lodged square into the side of Nelm's head, near the temple, ranging diagonally backward, and he fell dead. The other two men, who were unarmed, quietly surrendered.

Nelms' body was picked up and a navy six found clutched in his hand, the weapon lying under his body, he having fallen forward upon his face. It was a close call for Chief of Police Davis, and he did not act too promptly. The dead man was taken up and laid in the skiff, and within ten minutes after landing, the entire party were on their way back to the city. The inanimate body now lies in a plain pine coffin in the courtyard of the city prison. An inquest will be held later. Riley, Nelms' uncle, is in the calaboose and talks freely. SOLD HIS FARM.

Some days ago the father of the dead murderer sold his farm, a quarter section of land situated two miles from the river, near Norfolk, in Desoto county, Miss. The purchaser was Mr. J. T. La Prade, a popular citizen of Star Landing, and on Thursday last that gentleman paid its former owner $560 in cash for the realty subject to a previous mortgage upon it. Nelms' father went down the river from this city last Tuesday to close up his interests in the old homestead.

Mr. W. H. Rawlings, an officer connected with the jail at Senatobia, arrived in the city this morning and identified the body of Nelms. Jim Riley arrested at the time Nelms was killed, is the latter's uncle by marriage. He claims that he had been advised of Nelms' probable coming some days ago, and he expected him to arrive by the M. & C. railway.

At the time Nelms escaped from the Senatobia prison a few nights since, four other prisoners got away. One named Jim Morris, col'd, was recaptured and returned to his former quarters. Morris was under a charge of horse stealing. Another of the escaped prisoners named Lewis Flower, charged with petty larceny, was also retaken here a day or two since. It was from these that Captain Davis ascertained, or surmised, that Nelms would be harbored in this city, perhaps by his mother, who lives at the house of a Mr. Bacon, on Alabama street, in the southern part of the city.

One of the colored jurors who served at the time Nelms was last convicted, called at the station house.
NELMS' CRIME
was the killing of Mr. Rufus Armistead, manager on the plantation of Mr. Ed Hart, fourteen miles south of this city, on the evening of May 9th, 1880. The act was committed about 8 o'clock, just after dark. While Armistead was on his way from the stock lot to the house, Nelms, from an ambush, shot him just as he passed through the gate, the load tearing his stomach fearfully, and causing death in a few hours. Armistead had not done injury to Nelms, and indeed did not know him. Nelms had been employed by Mr. Hart in person that very day to do farm work, and had hardly spoken to Armistead. He evidently hired himself to Mr. Hart, with the intention of killing Armistead, as it was proven in trial that he had said he would have the blood of an Armistead if he had to kill a child to accomplish his end.

Nelms escaped at the time, but was subsequently captured in the cane brakes of Tunica county, after having been closely pursued for several days by dogs and men. He was in a half-starved condition and pretty well fagged out when taken. Several colored men who harbored Nelms in that vicinity were afterwards murdered by unknown persons, said to have been masked at the time, and the story is current that two of the slaughtered men were tied to the backs of their animals, with their stomachs upward, and their bowels were ripped open with butcher-knives. The perpetrators of these alleged diabolical acts have never been brought to justice.

After Nelm's arrest he was tried, convicted, and sentenced to be hung His case was appealed to the Supreme Court, which tribunal remanded it for a new trial. At the second trial he was again convicted and sentenced. The day arrived for his execution, and when the morning of it came, a telegram from Jackson, Miss., announced that the Supreme Court had again interfered, causing a stay of proceedings and a postponement of the hanging until the technicalities of the trial could be decided on.

Meantime the friends of Nelms busied themselves in his favor, and a few weeks ago his jailer awoke to find that he and four other prisoners had escaped in the darkness of the night, while he slumbered and dreamed.

Gray, interfered with a negro dance Monday night, and was fatally stabbed by three negro brothers, Bob. Henry and Alex. Jackson. Elijah Whitehead was killed by Turner Sutton, at Hawkinsville, Pulaski County, yesterday. Both were negroes.

She had been instructing the child how to aim the weapon, and sat down on the floor to play, when the child aimed the pistol and fired, the ball entering her brain. No one knew that the pistol was loaded.

ENGINEER'S REPORT.

"In relation to the petition of the Springfield and Memphis Railroad Company asking the Taxing-District to share one-third of the cost of a culvert which they propose to build in the bayou on Broadway street, in the Tenth ward, in constructing their line from Fifth street to a connection with the Mississippi and Tennessee railroad near Alabama, I submit herewith, as directed by your resolution, a plan and approximate estimate. The Memphis Avalanche of the 28th. contains a carefully prepared article beginning with these words: "Lynch law is anarchy. The rule of the mob is the nullification of the law. The Avalanche is opposed to a state of anarchy, because it is a condition destructive of all the interests which men can have in a country, &c.," and winds it up with, "It is a crime, which the Avalanche will not cease to denounce."

This is all right and in keeping with the teachings of a great and popular newspaper; but the fat of that article as it were, is knocked into the fire, by the very next one below it in the same column. It is introduced with a six inch double leaded heading, surmounted with a two-line pica sensational catch line which reads, "Retribution." Then follows a pen picture, in approved style, with sickening details, of the violation of the person of a young lady by a brutal negro, who threw his victim in a cistern. The water being too shallow to drown her, the negro slipped down the chain, and chucked her head under until she was drowned. He then then endeavored to climb up the chain to the mouth of the cistern, but this teat he was unable to perform, and was, so to speak, caught in his own trap. Here he was discovered and the neighbors gathered; he was drawn up, and with a rope and a convenient limb, short work was made with the limb, short work was made with the rapist. SATARTIA, Miss., July 25.

Our little village and the surrounding community was thrown into intense exaltement Sunday morning last upon hearing of a most brutal outrage committed upon the person of a young white girl, named Rosa Eatle, residing six miles from here, on the plantation known as Brown and Dalton, the deed being done by a negro man, named Isiah Fisher, working on the same place as a blacksmith.

On the morning of July 23rd the negro named above, watching his opportunity, seized the girl, and dragging her into his house, and there outraged her in the most brutal manner. After knocking her senseless, he dragged her to the cistern, only a short distance from the house, and after throwing her in, went back to his work. Not feeling satisfied that she was dead, he went to the cistern the second time, and finding her still alive, went down in the cistern, holding to the chain, there to finish his hellish work, choking and beating her, and then standing on her, body until the flendish work was complete, he being in the cistern at least an hour and a half. Finding he could not ascend the chain, he began calling for assistance, claiming he went there to save the young girl's life.

An inquest was held over the body of the dead girl Sunday morning, and the physician attending pronounced it, after careful examination, to be one of the most brutal outrages ever committed upon a female. The negro (Isiah Fisher) was arrested and brought to town Sunday night. The white and colored citizens held a meeting that night, some agreeing and others disagreeing as regards to the manner of his punishment. On Monday morning, Fisher having confessed he was guilty of the crime, about ten o'clock, the surrounding country, both black and white, with out further delay, swung him to the nearest tree, just outside of our village, where he remained hanging until two o'clock the same day. The body was then lowered, and the verdict of the coroner's jury was that said Fisher came to his death by hanging. There was about three hundred persons present.

Wife Murder in Ohio.

BELLEFONTAINE, O., Oct. 1.—On the Lewis-town and Bellefontaine turnpike, eight miles from Bellefontaine, occurred yesterday afternoon one of the most horrible affairs that has ever blackened the history of this country. Jacob Whitmore, a farmer about 28 years of age, was married on the 17th of July to Orrie Short, 14 years of age, the daughter of a widow. Yesterday afternoon Whitmore took his girl-wife out into the woods to gather huckory nuts, accompanied by her little brother and sister. Whitmore soon returned, and was followed in a short time by his wife, who was suffering from horrible cramps accompanied by spasms. A physician was summoned, but she died about midnight in terrible agony. At first the poor girl denied that anything was wrong with her, but when she found that death could not be arrested, she confessed that her husband had compelled her to take a white powder, threatening to cut her throat if she refused. Whitmore is a country youth, and told the Times correspondent to night, when interviewed in jail, that his wife killed herself. His preliminary examination takes place on Monday, and if the evidence is strong against him he may be lynched, as occurred here a few years ago in the notorious Shell case, the people being terribly incensed.

At the inquest on Saturday it was testified that Whitmore bought strychnine two weeks ago; that he said a few days ago that his wife should not be alive in a week. The little brother of the girl-wife testified in his childish way, confirming his sister's statement that Jake made her swallow the poison "or he would cut her throat." A piece of paper was also found in the woods with strychnine adhering to it, where the villain had forced her to take it. The sheriff has carried the prisoner to an adjoining county to escape the mob which he had been notified would hang Whitmore tonight. The town is filling up rapidly with excited men and neighbors of the girl to assist in the hanging, but they have come on a fruitless errand.

OHIO STATE NEWS.
THE suicidal mania seems to be looking up.

The ground was whitened with snow in Union County on the 24th.

Miss McAloon, a young lady of New Straitsville, was killed by a runaway team.

Henrick D. Leach, a young man of Canal Dover, suicided by shooting himself twice through the body.

Daniel Mullen, aged fifty years, was instantly killed by a passenger train at Youngstown. He leaves a large family.

On Sugar Run, near Pomeroy, George Fisher was fatally stabbed by Andrew Habrecht. Habrecht is in jail.

A young man of Dresden, Homer Bagent, was perhaps fatally stabbed by some unknown person while in a crowd of roughs.

George Vogel, a young man living near Millersburg, who was suicid last summer, has been declared insane and taken to Columbus.

Eaton, West Alexandria, Elkton, Winchester, Germantown, Miamisburg, Franklin, Middletown, and Lebanon are all connected by telephone.

Rev. Theodore Crowl, pastor of the Second P. esbyterian Church at Zanesville, was married the past week to Miss Mary C. Hobart, of Grinneil, Iowa.

Mrs. RENNING, of Braceville, Trumbull County, suicided by drowning. Her body was found floating in the river about six miles north of Warren.

Mr. Wesley Shanrer, of Green Springs, committed suicide by shooting himself through the heart with a double-barrel shotgun. Cause unknown.

George Baldwin, of Benton Ridge, died from the effects of strychnine administered by his own hand, but whether with suicidal intent is not known.

A twelve-year-old son of Dr. Landis, at Oberlin, who a few day ago shot himself accidentally with a toy pistol, has died from the effects of the wound.

The Commissioners of Perry County have purchased forty acres of land just west of New Lexington, on the Lancaster road, upon which to build a Children's Home.

Adam Kuntz, a respected farmer living two miles south of Galloway, suicided by cutting his wrist and throat with a razor. Cause, despondency over the death of a favorite daughter.

The John Mitchell furniture building, on Second street, between John and Smith st eets, Cincinnati, burned the past week entailing a loss on property and stock of $50,000, partially insured.

Miss Laura Gray, of Hudson, Summit County, who was some time ago disappointed in a love affair, has become violently insane. Miss Gray is aged twenty years, is handsome, and I am been popular in young society.

AT BELLEFONTAINE the Grand Jury indicted Jacob Whitmore for murder in the first degree, charged with poisoning his wife. Albert Hoge was also indicted for murder in the first degree, the crime charged being that of shooting Charles Martin to death.

NEAR Careysville, Champaign County, while returning from a church concert, three persons in buggies driving abreast on the pike, racing their horses, ran over a Miss Rosa Jenkins, a young lady who was walking in the road, and severely, if not fatally, injured her. She was badly bruised, and at last accounts in a precarious condition.

SAYS a Mount Vernon correspondent: Great anxiety prevails among farmers relative to wheat planted in September. Heavy rains and warm weather have caused it to prematurely advance, and it is claimed that fully one-half the amount sown is rotating at the roots or being destroyed by the Hessian fly. The abundant clover crop promised has not panned out, and the granger wears an elongated face and azure countenance.

J. R. Muzem, of Barnesville, Belmont County, some days ago, started on his way to Milwaukee to wed an estimable young lady of that city. While en route he stopped at Chicago to see the sights. Drinking was of course a part of the programme, and it is stated that when Mr. Muzem wound up in the station-house on the verge of lunacy from excess of drink, it was found his spree had cost him $1,900. Mr. Muzem is well advanced in years, and well to do. He does not often drink, but when he does, everybody in his region is apt to find it out.

MRS. MARY FRY, the wife of a well-to-do farmer living north of Unionville, eloped with Jed Davis, a young man living with Fry as a farm hand. Davis left a note saying he was aware of the enormity of his offense, but Mary had mashed him, and he was powerless to resist the temptation. Mrs. Fry added a brief, business-like postscript, urging her husband to procure a decree of divorce right away and marry a certain widowed lady of the neighborhood, who, she was quite sure, would be good to the seven small Fry she was leaving to his care.

A STRANGER on horseback stopped at the farm-house of Fred Eaglehoff, five miles north of Plain City, and, after eating dinner and smoking with the farmer, made a proposition to trade horses, his being an excellent one, and soon after put his saddle on Eaglehoff's horse and rode it to try its speed, he said. Since Eaglehoff has seen neither stranger nor horse. On the evening of the same day a second party, claiming to come from Southern Ohio, called and laid claim to the stranger's horse as property stolen from him two nights before. Eaglehoff looked on the matter as a put-up job and refused to give up the animal.

The Servo-American treaty has been signed.
Michigan relief fund in New York, $107,-922.

The British troops are returning from Afghanistan.

The general convention of Universalists is in session at Detroit.

Senators Ingalls and Garland are preparing a national bankruptcy bill.

Owners at Copenhagen of the steamer Thingvallo think she is safe.

Preparations are making at Moscow for the coronation of Alexander III.

Electric lighting of cars on the London & Brighton railway is successful.

Secretary Windom has received $50 from Cleveland for the conscience fund.

Baron Haymerle's death postponed the czar's interview with Francis Joseph.

Ex-Gov. Fairchild, late minister to Spain, will not return to this country until spring.

Gen. Banks says he knows nothing of his alleged appointment as governor of Arizona.

Assim Pasha, minister of foreign affairs for Turkey, insists upon resigning his portfolio.

The fifth annual meeting of the American Humane association commenced yesterday in Boston.

Delegates to choose senators will be elected in France November 20. The final election is January 8.

A Fargo telegram says the rumor that King's balloon had been seen in that vicinity is unfounded.

Printer Defrees did not shut the printing office for the Yorktown holiday, and the employees complain.

The National carriage builders' association met at Cincinnati yesterday, President J. M. Bristow in the chair.

A Zanzibar dispatch says: The Belgian expedition under Rogers, with 135 natives, sails to-morrow to join Stanley on the Congs.

The fish commission steamer Fishhawk, has brought a large whale skeleton from Provincetown, Mass., for the national museum.

The ninth annual congress for the advancement of women opened yesterday at Buffalo. Delegates were present from all parts of the Union.

A North Walden, Vt., farmer writes Treasurer Gilfillan asking if $225 of notes which his cow chewed can be redeemed. They can if distinguishable.

The five experts appointed by the general association of underwriters of the United States to examine the fire department of St. Louis, have begun work.

About 10:30 yesterday morning J. B. Ames, a prominent miller of Sandusky, O., in trying to run a belt from a fly-wheel, was caught in the machinery and instantly killed.

The ninth annual meeting of Union prisoners occurred at Springfield, Ill., yesterday. It was attended by something over 200 prisoners of war, and many other veteran soldiers.

Owing to the discharge of a favorite foreman, 400 strippers in Lorillard's tobacco factory, Jersey City, are on a strike. This action of the girls causes the enforced idleness of 200 men.

The Albany, N. Y., Evening Journal says Judge Folger has had no authoritative information of the intention of the president to call him to assume the portfolio of the treasury department.

Harvey, owner of the Randolph mills, Philadelphia, found criminally responsible for loss of life in neglecting to furnish fire escapes, has been committed to await the action of the district attorney.

At Louisville, yesterday, a dog fight occurred between Pilot, of New York city, and Crib, of Louisville, for $1,000 a side. Pilot won after a battle of an hour, which ended in the death of the Louisville dog.

An order was entered and bond for $10,000 given in the United States circuit court at St. Louis yesterday, appointing John M. Douglas receiver of the Ohio & Mississippi railroad property within the jurisdiction of the court.

Randolph Disbrow, of the New Jersey battalion, had both hands blown off by the premature discharge of a cannon at Yorktown, yesterday. Both arms were amputated. The governor of New Jersey says Disbrow will be pensioned.

The annual session of the International brotherhood of locomotive engineers, assembled at Baltimore yesterday, with a full attendance of delegates from the United States and Canada. P. M. Arthur, grand chief engineer, of Cleveland, presided.

WACO, TEXAS., October 20.—Kit Hunston, who was stabbed at Hillsboro, by James Everett, is dead and Everett is in jail.

Murdered by Negroes.

McKINNEY, TEXAS, October 20.—Mr. Nowel, a well-to-do farmer, was murdered at his residence by a negro named Zach Lind-say and an unknown man. Cause—quarrel over a business transaction.

Died in the Line of His Duty.

PRESCOTT, ARIZ., October 20.—Deputy-Sheriff Briant was killed while in the discharge of his duty by a desperado named Miller. The murderer escaped. A large force is in search.

Went Through a Sleeper.

St. LOUIS, October 20.—George F. Roberts, an Englishman, was robbed of $1900 in a sleeping-car between Indianapolis and Litch-field, on the Indianappolis and St. Louis Road. Five other passengers were robbed of small sums.

Road Agents in Texas.

HENRIETTA, TEXAS, October 20.—The mail coach from Gainesville was stopped at East Belknap, twenty miles east of here, and the driver compelled to cut open the mail bags. This is the fourth time the mail has been robbed by road agents on this route.

How Mitchell was Killed.

SAN FRANCISCO, October 20.—A Bakerfield dispatch says that Deputy-Sheriff Mitchell, who was shot by a mob last night, met the crowd as they approached the jail. Nearly all of them were drunk. Shots were at once exchanged, and Mitchell was almost instantly killed. He shot one of his assailants. The crowd then dispersed without accomplishing their object, that of lynching Herbert.

Missouri Train Robbers.

St. Louis, October 20.—At Independence John Bugler and John Land were arraigned in the Criminal Court, upon indictments charging them with participation in the Chicago and Alton train robbery. Both pleaded not guilty, and their trials were postponed until the next term of the court. Bail was fixed at $4200 each. Creed Chapman, one of the leaders of the gang, will be arraigned Saturday.

On the Ground of Insanity.

PHILADELPHIA, October 20.—In the trial of George Wood, charged with throwing vitriol into the face of George Sheppard, by which the latter was terribly burned and lost one eye, the jury returned a verdict of not guilty on the ground of the insanity of the defendant at the time of the commission of the act. The Judge said it remained with him to decide whether Wood should not be confined in an institution for the insane if he has not yet recovered his reason.

The McGrail Murderer.

The McGrain Murderer.

Columbus, O., October 20.—William Bray and John O'Neil have been arrested on suspicion of murdering the soldier, Charles P. McGrail, on Monday morning. Bray was arrested yesterday, but no charge was preferred against him until to-day, when he was accused of murder in the second degree. No charge has been preferred against O'Neil. The murder has caused considerable excitement in this city, which has resulted in severe charges against some members of the police force for neglect of duty.

An Illinois Bank Robbery.

JERSEYVILLE, ILL., October 20.—Charles Clay and John Burrus went into Wesley Park & Sons bank, at Fieldon, at 2 oclock to-day, and at the muzzle of two revolvers compelled Mr. Park to open his safe and give them $5500. The robbers then mounted their horses and rode away. Park followed them to the street and fired upon them, killing one of their horses. The dismounted robber got on the horse of his pal and both of them rode off together. Sheriff Massey raised a posse, and is now scouring the county for the robbers, who it is said cannot escape.

Another Good Man Gone Wrong.

KENOSHA, Wis., October 20.—Herbert Theirs, of this city, has committed forgeries to the amount of $60,000 in mortgages and notes. Among others, he made a duplicate of a mortgage on E. Pennoyer for $14,000, and played the same trick on others in amounts of three and four thousand dollars. A number of other misdeeds have been discovered. He left town at noon to-day, and early in the afternoon the entire matter was discovered. He was a highly respected member of one of the Kenosha churches. No trace of him has yet been discovered.

LOUISIANA LYNCH-LAW.
The Columbia Herald gives particulars of a case of incendiarism in Jackson parish. The residence of Mr. Fuller was set on fire last April, while thirteen persons were in the house—coal oil having been poured here and there to facilitate the work of conflagration. Two colored persons, a man and a woman, were subsequently arrested on suspicion; and the evidence against the man was very strong. He broke jail and escaped before indictment; and the jury failed to agree as to the guilt of the woman, there being eleven for conviction and one for acquittal. Subsequently in the latter part of August the fugitive negro was rearrested, taken out of jail by a mob, and hung to a tree.

The crime was a peculiarly fiendish one, for all the inhabitants of the house might have been burnt alive. The evidence was strong against the lynched negro; and there is every probability that had he been tried, he might have been acquitted through the stupidity or partizanship of a mixed jury. But it is nevertheless to be deprecated that such a course should have been pursued until his guilt was settled beyond all shadow of doubt. And there are always schemers ready and eager to coin political capital out of such occurrences.

But it must be remembered that in certain parts of Louisiana the whites must rule with a rod of iron in order to preserve law and order. In Jackson there is a small white majority; but there are parishes in which the black majority is enormous. The two great crimes to which the blacks are most prone under the influence of passion are rape and arson; crimes which ought in all civilized countries to be invariably punished with death. Then there is the cause of the jury farce. A mixed jury will seldom convict a negro of a serious offense, when that offense has been perpetrated against some one not of their own color. But law must nevertheless hold its own: and the ignorant mass of negroes must learn that the intelligent portion of the population in their parish can rule, and will be masters, and will enforce the penalties of the law in spite of the abnormal condition of affairs. Therefore, while it is possible that the lynchers of the incendiary in Jackson acted overhastily, we can hardly blame them if they were positive that they had the right man.

In a few years more, however, there will be an end of such scandals and such horrors; but the black population will sink to a natural level of numerical inferiority. The parishes will be thickly settled; men from the North and East and West will pour into Louisiana, while from the South Spanish and French emigration will swell the white population. Until an increase of population and capital, and a consequent increase of prosperity, law will be so well established that the public need not fear that any such crimes as rape and arson will be suffered to go unpunished by the courts. It is the distrust of legal authority that often leads unauthorized men, as it did in the above case, to take law into their own hands. N. O. Item.

MISSING.
A St. Joseph special says: The fourth or fifth mysterious disappearance within a year has just taken place. The missing man is Walter C. Bailey, shipping clerk in the house of Turner, Frisco & Co. He disappeared last Tuesday and has not been heard of since. He was suffering from a temporary aberration of the brain, probably produced by malerial fever. Last Tuesday he attempted to shoot a lady and gentleman in the St. Charles hotel, and fired, but the ball passed through the clothing of the persons. The revolver was taken from him. He demanded it two or three times but it was refused. Since then nothing has been seen or heard of him.

FEARFUL EXPLOSION.

JERSEY CITY, Sept. 13.—A bay boiler exploded this morning at Bulman & Brown's dock at the foot of Essex street. Capt. Decker, of the tug Gladwish, and Jas. Tamman, were instantly killed, and two or three others fatally injured. The boiler was blown 600 feet up Essex street. In its course it cut down a lamp post and five hydrants. Two large trees and two wagons standing in the street were entirely destroyed. A horse and cart of John Adam's which his son, aged 11, was driving, was struck by the flying boiler, the vehicle and horse literally cut to pieces, and the boy's right leg severed from his body. Cause of explosion, carelessness.

ARKANSAS LYNCHERS JUSTIFIED.

LITTLE Rock, Ark., Sept. 13.—News is received that Saturday night a hundred men rode to the jail at Dorbanville, and took the two murderers, Taylor and Bruce, dragged them into the woods with ropes about their necks and to a patch of timber, where they left them dangling to trees. The men were bruised and lifeless before they reached the scene of their death. Both died defying their executioners. This sort of thing is becoming common in this section and public opinion is with the lynchers, owing to the loose administration of justice in the courts.

TWO MURDERERS HUNG.
We are informed that Messrs. Taylor and Bruce, of Yell county, were both taken from the Dardaneille jail on Saturday night and hung. This is a terrible precedent and opens the door for unauthorized and arbitrary violence and merits the condemnation of all good law abiding citizens. The long delays by the courts, the very many technicalities of the law so common and invariably resorted to for postponing the trial of criminals, the injudicious and too frequently extended clemency of the pardoning power of the executive, the many escapes from the jails of the country, together with the wholesale delivery by the sheriff or guard (the very officers of the law whose duty it was to keep secure and not to liberate) from the Ozark jail so many men and prisoners who had in cold blood murdered Burgess James in Yell county, entailing in addition to this horrible and atrocious deed upon her citizens, a very large, heavy and extraordinary bill of costs in their prosecution, all of which has doubtless for the reasons and causes enumerated been the incentive to action of those engaged in this objectionable and arbitrary tragedy and which it is said from rumor was composed of some of the very best and heretofore law abiding citizens of Yell county. Until a different course shall be pursued by the courts in giving speedier trials, the abandonment of technicalities resorted to by attorneys for delays and postponements, and less extension and clemency of the pardoning power of the executive of the state, with a more rigid care and safe keeping of prisoners by officers of the law, whose duty it is to secure and not liberate them, we need not expect a correction or abandonment of the greatly to be deplored evils of mob violence and lynch law.

Ex-Minister Christianity was robbed of $6,000 worth of diamonds and jewelry in his strong box in his room, in the National hotel, Washington. The thieves forced the door and secured the plunder during Christianity's temporary absence. The jewels were not the property of Christianity, but left with him for safe-keeping. It is believed the thieves followed Christianity from New York.

It is claimed that six of the Glendale train-robbers have been captured. They prove to be young farmers living in the immediate vicinity of the outrage, and the idea that the James brothers were in the raid has been quite generally abandoned. Matt Chapman gave to a sheriff the names of the robbers, and has himself been placed in jail at Independence as a witness.

A party of armed and mounted men took from the jail at Dardenelle, Ark, two murders named John Taylor and J. F. Bruce, and hanged them in an adjacent grove. The reason of the lynching was that the prisoners were likely to escape justice by changes of venue.

Two young planters of Booneville, Ark, named William and Robert Hambery, were shot by parties in ambush along the roadside. The latter was instantly killed and the former mortally wounded. Two negroes have been arrested on suspicion.

Jane Campbell, a colored woman living near Dycke's Mills, La., killed her two children, aged 10 and 12, by beating their brains out with pine knots for some trivial act of disobedience. A mob took the woman from jail and burned her at the stake.

MOB LAW.
It is with a great deal of regret that we observe the growing popularity of Judge Lynch in our State. His visits are becoming so frequent as to excite solicitude in the breast of all good citizens. Week before last his terrible power was exerted upon a victim in Jackson county, and also in Yell county his swift judgement was visited upon two. We are not thoroughly posted as to the details of the crimes charged against any of the parties, but do not think from our information that they were of that agravated form which somehow or other it meets with partial public favor to visit with such swift and condign punishment outside the forms of law.

It has never been eradicated from the minds of the people to wreak vengeance upon certain base and wicked crimes committed in their midst, but in our country the exercise of this frightful power has been principally confined to the few cases that shock public morals and outrage the principles of virtue. The cases before us are exceptions to this rule. They fell in the line of murder—a crime which is dark and wicked, 't is true, but one which has always been accorded a hearing and final adjudication in the courts, and we know of nothing in any of these cases that would take them out of the line of crimes of this sort. The inquiry then arises, what is the matter, and where is the trouble?

Is the fault with the people? We are loth to believe it. They have possibly allowed themselves to some extent to be thrown into a state of solicitude by the tardiness of justice in our courts in which they have come to think that public safety lies in their dealing out to criminals that which lies in the jurisdiction of courts to give, but which they have been so prone of late to escape. What the people want, and what they demand, is that crime shall be punished. And we look upon these occurrences not so much as a spirit of mob law, as an attestation of this def mand. The heavy cost of criminal prosecution, the endless delays of justice and the final escape of the criminal, have conspired to make justice a byword and punishment for crime a mockery. In this state of the case, much as we may regret it, it is not surprising that occasionally the feeling should show itself beyond the limits of prudence, to enforce obedience to the demand that the law must be enforced.

It's an unpleasant sentence to write in which responsibility for this state of feeling is placed anywhere, and especially with those in whose hands is the administration of law. We think, however, that we take no risk in the proposition that with a vigorous, speedy and certain execution of the law, our eyes would never have seen the particulars of these occurrences.

MERIDIAN, MISS., Nov. 8, 1831.
Capt. FRANK JOHNSTON:
Dear Sir:—Condition of affairs in our county is appalling tonight. This has been a dreadful day with our people. Some of our citizens slaughtered—victims of the "six-barrelled code" doctrine. The Democrats are entirely blameless, and (please excuse the expression,) d——d be he who first cries "The Democrats are to blame for it!" The circumstances, in brief, are these:
This morning, as an old white gentleman at Marion was going in to cast his vote he was grossly insulted by one of the most impudent negroes in the county, who had come to Marion from his own voting place, which was another Box. "Lyle's Store." The insult caused the old man to raise his arm as if to repel it with a blow, when a number of negroes immediately fired on him with pistols, killing him instantly. Then A. T. Harvey, Democratic candidate for Assessor, rushed up, unarmed and was shot down and instantly killed; then Harvey's brother-in-law, Joseph Barrett, was killed in the same way; then a man named Jeff Segars—all four good white men instantly killed when they had not a weapon to defend themselves with. Vince Segars and James Hodges, both white men, were seriously wounded, the former with but little hope of recovery. On hearing of it here the Sheriff left on a special train with a posse of about a hundred men, but they found the groes, about a hundred in number, had taken refuge in the dwelling house of Ed. Vance, a notorious Republican, where they together with Vance, and his two sons, William and John, were prepared to make a desperate defense. Our boys were repulsed, and had to come back here for reinforcements. Another crowd from here joined the sheriff, and about 5 o'clock this afternoon the sheriff, with a hundred men or more, arrived there, and was preparing to surround it, when the wife of Vance came to the front gate with a white flag. The sheriff communicated with her, and offered to protect her husband and all in his house, if they would surrender. This being agreed to, some of our boys entered the yard, and were drinking water from the well, anticipating no danger, when one man in the sheriff's party at the well, was shot by some one from the inside of the house, and instantly killed. His name was Mr. Warren, a clerk in Meridian, in the store of Fincher & McMichael. His body will be brought in to-night on the mail train. John Vance, the son of Ed Vance, was killed, and William Vance was captured, and is now lodged in jail. Ed Vance managed to escape by way of the back door, while his wife was offering the flag of truce at the front, and while a number of negroes also escaped, several were shot by the sheriff's posse, as they ran through the bushes. The sheriff himself was hit by a spent bullet in the side, but it is not painful or inconvenient.

Our town is in gloom to-night, especially over the sudden news of Warren's death. Excuse this illegible scribbling. I am writing by a dim light in the back room of a drug store. While on the streets knots of men talk about desperate things that suggest blood. Everything will pass off quietly though. Meridian box at this hour counts out about 5 for Lowry to King's one. Yours truly,

For the first time in twenty-odd years, we believe, the Democrats have elected a majority of both branches of the Legislature. This is a marked instance of the mutability of politics. THE BOTTOM FACTS OF THE MISSISSIPPI MASSACRE. How Colored Men Were Shot Down at the Polls and the Facts Distorted and Sent by Wire to the Country—The Work of Bourbon Devils.
MERIDIAN, Miss., Dec. 10.—After its usually comprehensive style, THE REPUBLICAN has frequently cautioned its readers against receiving as true the reports coming through Democratic sources of the late election riot at Marion Station, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, where a number of white Democrats were killed by colored men and Republicans. Marion is only five miles from Meridian, the county seat, where the writer of this resided nearly four years, and, being well acquainted with most of the persons named in the dispatch in connection with the so-called massacre, I have taken great pains to learn the bottom facts in regard to it, and here present them as they come to me through the most reliable and trustworthy sources. My informants, some of them eye-witnesses, embrace every shade of politics; all live near the scene of the riot, and agree as to the main facts.

LAUDERDALE IS HOPELESSLY DEMOCRATIC, but the precinct of Marion Station, when a free vote and a fair count can be had, is largely Republican, and it is the only Republican precinct in the county; hence at every election since the organization of the party in the State there has been "trouble" at Marion. It appears from good Democratic authority that "trouble" was anticipated on the day of the late election. This will be seen from the following: "We encountered a squad of young men of the city last night who are intent upon going to Marion to the election to-day. We think they mean business; and every one of them has a white skin, and, we believe, a white heart. They will keep the peace there themselves to-day, and see to it that everybody else does. They are true, and some on elections."—Mercury (Meridian, Miss.), November 8.

ONE OF THESE "YOUNG MEN"

who went to Marion on that day, being "some on elections," was Moore, the foreman of the Mercury office. Moore has acted as a bully and general fighting man for the Mercury for the past eight or nine years, the editor himself having no capacity whatever for that branch of the profession, though in Mississippi it is the most essential qualification of an editor. It is a melancholy feature in reviewing this matter to learn that Moore escaped with a slight wound. The two Seagers brothers spoken of in the dispatches, one of whom was killed at the polls that day and the other mortally wounded, were young drunken desperadoes, one of them but a few weeks before he was killed having murdered a colored man in cold blood, but escaping the gallows on the ground of "temporary insanity, superinduced by the use of intoxicating liquor." Harvey, candidate for assessor, who also lived at Meridian, was the only one killed at the polls that day whose loss the community will mourn. Joe Barnett, spoken of in the dispatches as an "innocent old man," and the first victim of the slaughter,

WAS THE ONLY DEMOCRAT KILLED

who belonged in Marion or had any legitimate business there other than that foreshadowed by the Mercury. This "innocent old man" (about forty years of age) was the prime mover of the difficulty, as he was first to pay the penalty. When the polls opened, at nine o'clock in the morning, says an eye-witness, there were about forty whites and seventy-five colored men on the ground. Barnett carried a cudgel about two inches in diameter and three feet long, which he used in the most approved Bourbon style. As the situation became more alarming the colored men huddled together some thirty yards distant from the polls, Barnett and Harvey and these young devils from Meridian following them up with sticks and pistols in their hands.
ABOUT THIS TIME BARNETT STEPPED UP to a colored man named Gillespie and demanded his ticket. Upon his refusal to comply with this demand Barnett struck Gillespie with his club, knocking him down. When Gillespie rose from the ground he seized a brickbat. Then Barnett drew his pistol and Gillespie retreated. Some one held Barnett and prevented him from shooting. When Gillespie returned some four or five of his colored friends and relatives gathered round him, apart from the body of colored men assembled. While thus awaiting developments they were confronted by about an equal number of whites, headed by Barnett and the two Seagers, when the fight began in earnest, Seagers firing the first shot

ONE COLORED MAN—ALEX. BROWN—did nearly or quite all the shooting for the colored side. When the smoke of battle had cleared the polls were deserted, and not a colored man was to be found on the ground, but the bloody corpses of the Mercury's "young men" lying here and there told too well the result of the contest. Ed. Vance, an honest, plodding, hard-working Irishman, who lived some three miles from his voting-place at Marion, at once took refuge with his two young boys in his own house. A few negroes living on Vance's place, becoming alarmed, went into the house with Vance for safety, those who did the shooting at Marion having ridden off in another direction. Vance, it may be well to mention in this connection, was a loyal man during the war, and has been a Republican ever since, in consequence of which his persecutions have been enough to drive any man to desperation.

IT WAS DOUBTLESS THOUGHT by the Democrats that a good opportunity now offered for setting the Vances out of the way, as they were becoming quite an important factor in the politics of the county. Accordingly they rallied in large numbers, surrounded Vance's house, and demanded the surrender of all within. The demand was not complied with, Vance being master of the situation, until the sheriff arrived with reinforcements from Meridian, at which time a parley ensued, Mrs. Vance coming out with a white flag and acting as spokeswoman. Warren, of the sheriff's posse, approached Mrs. Vance in an angry and threatening manner, with pistol in hand. Just at this time the eldest of Vance's sons, who had not been engaged in the melee at all, riding up from the outside, was shot dead by the sheriff's posse. Seeing his brother shot down and his mother's life being threatened, one of the young brothers from inside the house shot and killed Warren. Vance, it is supposed, then fled from the rear of the house, followed by the colored men who were barricaded with him, but in doing so a number of the latter were shot and killed.

VANCE IS STILL SECRETED IN THE WOODS, and one of his sons, with some eight or ten negroes, are in the Meridian jail. What their fate will be is hard to tell at this time, but it is generally conceded now that Vance had nothing whatever to do with the trouble at Marion Station. It is important to state in connection with this affair that the Republicans had no ticket in the field in Lauderdale County, and gave only a negative support to what is known there as the "Anti-Monopolists." Consequently there could have been no unusual inducement for Republicans to have precipitated a riot on the day of the election. It is no more than justice to say that Henderson, the sheriff has acted fairly and manfully throughout in this matter, and it is doubtless owing to his influence that scores of lives have been saved since that fatal day.

Frank and John McDonald, two ex-convicts who have just completed an eighteen-months' term in the State prison, and have been out only two weeks, while at a disreputable house in the outskirts of this village, day before yesterday, got into a row with Willie Kittson, a half-breed, about 23 years old. CANON CITY Described by a Memphian - A Pretty Good Place, But -.
About eight months ago I bade farewell to your beautiful city, which had been my home for several years. I had determined to "Go West, young man, and grow up with the country." So on the 25th day of November last I found myself dumped off a narrow-gauge coach at the base of the Rockies, in the town of Canon City, Colorado, where I have resided ever since. Canon City lies singly at the base of the Foot Range, whose rugged peaks tower to a hight of 2500 feet above the city, and act as forerunners for the snowy range that lies forty miles beyond. The Arkansas at this point breaks through the mountains and forms the Grand Canon, with its Royal Gorge. The little river, Grape creek, here joins the Arkansas with one of the most beautiful canons on earth. The Arkansas Valley here widens out into one of the most charming and fertile of the Colorado parks. About forty miles to the north towers in majestic grandeur the snowy summit of Pike's Peak. Within two hours walk from Canon City is the Royal Gorge of the Arkansas, whose rock walls rise 2000 feet in perpendicular height. The scenery in the vicinity of Canon City varies from the beautiful and lovely to a sublimity that is perfectly awful. Canon City has a population of about twenty-five hundred souls, and is growing rapidly. Her streets are broad avenues, crossing each other at right angles, and are bordered on either side with trees. Every gutter runs as a constant stream of clear water, which gives fertility to her many gardens. Her buildings are mostly of stone or brick, and are very substantial. The city is supplied with pure water from the never-failing Arkansas, and she expects soon to have her streets and halls lighted with gas or electricity. At present there are in course of construction brick and stone buildings which will aggregate a cost of $100,000. The mineral springs of Canon City, in medicinal properties, are not excelled by any in the State. Her soda and

iron springs are almost ice cold, while the hot springs afford a most delicious bath. No place in the United States enjoys a finer and more health-giving climate than Canon City. Her winter days are more like spring than winter, while the summer is never oppressive. It is true that this climate is subject to great and sudden changes, but the extreme dryness, purity and lightness of the atmosphere prevent any serious effect on the human system. Indeed, Canon City has long been a favorite winter resort for the mountaineer, as well as a summer resort for the States. Her altitude of 5000 feet above the sea level tempers the summer heat, and the lofty mountains, to the west and north, softens the rigor of her winters. The region to which Canon City looks for support, and which will, sooner or later, make her a beautiful city, I will set forth in another communication. For the present I will only say that Colorado is not without objections, and I would advise no Tennessee to sacrifice or dispose of a comfortable home with the expectation of finding a better here. What is a paradise for some is a hell for others.

W. J. MILLER.

CHEROKEES

Dropping Into the Political Methods of the Whites.

Special to the Appeal.]

LITTLE ROCK, August 2.—The Indians in the Cherokee Nation, Indian Territory, held a general election yesterday, and selected forty members of the National Council and seventeen of the Grand Council, all for two years. A solicitor, judge and sheriff were also elected in each of the nine districts. There were two tickets—National and Union—in the field, but, in fact, no difference in the platform of the parties, the struggle being the "outs" against the "ins." The returns indicate that the offices are about equally divided. Considerable excitement prevailed, and there were many rows, but no killing. The newly-elected members of the National and Grand Councils will begin their terms of office on the first Monday in November.

WILL THEY NEVER LEARN

That Almost Certain Death Awalts Perpetration of the Crime?

RUTHERFORD, TENN., August 2.—On Sunday night, in the town of Dyersburg, Tennessee, between 12 and 1 o'clock, Mike Wells, colored, entered the house of Mrs. Childs, widow of J. F. Childs, and endeavored to ravish her in the most cruel manner, choking her severely and smothering her with his hands to keep her from giving any alarm; but before he accomplished his hellish intent she succeeded in giving an alarm, which frightened the villain and brought to her rescue a young man who was rooming close by her residence. By this time the scoundrel had made his escape. The young man hastily notified the police force, which by 4 o'clock yesterday morning, headed by Ex-Sheriff Nichols, succeeded in arresting the criminal, who was placed under guard until between 10 and 11 o'clock, when he was taken possession of by an indignant mob, who meted out to him in the Courthouse yard that punishment he so justly deserved, and there he hung to a limb until he was dead, dead, dead.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES-BY TELEGRAPH.
A MESSENGER BURNED TO DEATH.
PHILADELPHIA, Nov. 5. — Edward Burke, an American District Telegraph messenger, was burned to death this morning by the explosion of an oil lamp at the office at Broad and Chestnut-sts.

硫酸TED WITH A RAZOR.
BANGOR, Me., Nov. 5. — Charles R. Lewis, a negro, was arrested last night for assaulting John Nolan with a razor. Nolan identified him as his assailant, but Lewis denies all knowledge of the crime.

MORTALLY WOUNDED BY A NEGRO.
ATLANTA, Ga., Nov., 5. — A dispatch to The Constitution from Camak, Ga., says: "At a negro 'supper' near here a drunken negro shot and mortally wounded Elias Edwards, a respectable white citizen."

KILLED WHILE OUT HUNTING.
NEW-BRUNSWICK, Nov. 7. — Walter Seabring killed Henry Waters to-day, at Hope Villa, Madison Township, by the accidental discharge of his gun. He was out hunting, and while loading his gun, the hammer fell and the discharge entered Walter's brain.

KILLED IN RESISTING A SHERIFF.
LITTLE ROCK, Nov. 5. — Felix Burke, a negro, was killed yesterday, in Monroe County, by Deputy-Sheriff McDonald who was endeavoring to arrest him for stealing a male. A fierce pistol light occurred between the men, and McDonald was dangerously wounded.

A STUDENT MURDERER.

TIEPIN, O., November 5.—The preliminary trial of Charles Madder, a student, who murdered Miss Phoebe Bernard on Thursday night, because she declined to marry him, is in progress. A great deal of excitement is manifested, and fears are entertained that if the result of the trial is not satisfactory, Madder will be lynched.

KICKED TO DEATH.

NOT GUILTY.

NAPOLEON, Ohio, November 6.—At 11 a. m. the jury in the Gev. Scott murder case returned a verdict of not guilty.

A MULE THIEF KILLED.

CINCINNATI, November 6.—Little Rock special says that Deputy Sheriff McDonald shot and killed Felix Burell, a mule thief, during a running fight in Monroe county yesterday and McDonald was badly wounded. Burell stole a mule from a widow two months ago and yesterday came back and stole another.

TRAN MEN INDICTED.

SANFORD, Ky, November 6.—L. F. McNama, conductor, and Wm Taite, engineer of the train, that killed five men at McKinney, on the Cincinnati Southern Railway two weeks ago, have been indicted for murder in the first degree. They ran off immediately after the collision and have not since been heard of. The Governor will offer a reward for their capture.

SENTENCED TO BE HUNG.

A ROW IN CAMP.

COLUMBUS, Ga., November 6.—In the camp of Mr. English, on the P. & Railroad in Florida, a white man named Turnage and a colored man named Quinley engaged in an altercation. The other negroes took it up and at night fired into the camp, resulting in the death of a colored man and the wounding of other parties.

ROW AT A DANCE.

ATLANTA, Ga., November 6.—Several white men went to a negro dance near Carmad last night and got into drunken row with some negroes. Elias Edwards (white) was shot in the temple by Austin Howard, a negro, and killed. Another white man was not though not fatally. The negro escaped.
